Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

The opposing political parties nevertheless took a [bilateral] position in the national interest.
explanation: 'Bipartisan' means supported by two opposing political parties, which is exactly the sense of rival parties uniting in the national interest. 'Bilateral' means between two countries or sides in an agreement and is not used for a party position, and 'impartial' (unbiased) does not convey joint agreement.

text:
Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Although she had sampled food from all the restaurants in the food court, she remained [indefinite] towards the culinary fare on offer.
explanation: 'Indifferent' means having no particular interest or liking, which fits someone left unimpressed after tasting everything on offer. 'Indefinite' means vague or unlimited and cannot describe an attitude towards food, and 'imperious' (domineering) does not fit either.

text:
Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

The attitude of the whalers was marked by [antipathy] towards the marine life they had to encounter.
explanation: Whalers kill marine creatures as a trade, not out of personal hatred, so their attitude is best described as callous 'indifference' (lack of concern). 'Animus' is only a synonym of 'antipathy' and so improves nothing, while 'sympathy' and 'empathy' contradict the sense of the sentence.

text:
Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

The family was rendered [diligent] due to the crash in the share market.
explanation: 'Indigent' means poor or needy, which is the natural result of a share-market crash, and the verb 'rendered' calls for a resulting state like this. 'Diligent' means hardworking and makes no sense here, and 'indignant' (angry) does not describe being made poor.

text:
Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

He had cultivated such great temperance in his personality that he was [impassioned] in his dealing with the vicissitudes of life.
explanation: Someone who has cultivated 'temperance' (self-restraint) would be 'dispassionate', meaning calm and not swayed by emotion, when facing life's ups and downs. 'Impassioned' means full of strong emotion, the opposite of temperance, and 'perfunctory' means careless and done only for form's sake.

text:
Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

The document was discerned to be a [postscript], where clearly an earlier manuscript had been replaced by a new one.
explanation: A 'palimpsest' is a manuscript whose original writing was scraped off so it could be written over, which matches 'an earlier manuscript had been replaced by a new one'. A 'postscript' is a note added at the end of a letter, and a 'pastiche' is an imitation of another work's style.

text:
Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

He was accused of [simulism] for having copied from someone else without due acknowledgement.
explanation: 'Plagiarism' is copying another person's work and passing it off as your own without acknowledgement, exactly what the sentence describes. 'Simulism' is not a standard word, and a 'spoonerism' is an accidental swap of the first sounds of words (as in 'tease my ears' for 'ease my tears').

text:
Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

The domineering manager behaved in a [paternal] manner with his subordinates, not allowing them to decide for themselves.
explanation: 'Paternalistic' describes controlling people supposedly for their own good while denying them the freedom to decide, which fits a domineering manager. 'Paternal' just means fatherly or protective and lacks this sense of restriction, and 'presumptuous' (overstepping limits) does not capture it either.

text:
Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Much to their disappointment, the team leader spared no more than a [reflective] glance at the draft plan drawn up by his team.
explanation: A 'perfunctory' glance is quick and careless, made only as a formality, which explains why the team was disappointed. A 'reflective' glance would show careful thought, the opposite of what upset them.

text:
Directions: Each of the sentences in the following items has a word in square brackets, followed by four choices. Select the most appropriate option that improves/corrects the word in square brackets in the context of the sentence, and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Her actions were considered [salutary] because they were done without good reason or cause.
explanation: 'Gratuitous' means done without good reason or justification, which matches 'without good reason or cause'. 'Salutary' means beneficial, which contradicts the sentence, and 'grating' (irritating) does not fit the meaning.

Directions: Each item in this section has a sentence with three parts in square brackets labelled (a), (b) and (c). Read each sentence to determine whether there is an error in any part in square brackets and indicate your response on the answer sheet against the above-mentioned corresponding letter. [In his well-recognised stentorian yet amused voice] (a) [the principal demanded an unique excuse] (b) [from the student hauled up for alleged minor misdemeanour.] (c) [No error] (d)
a: In his well-recognised stentorian yet amused voice
b: the principal demanded an unique excuse
c: from the student hauled up for alleged minor misdemeanour.
explanation: The choice between 'a' and 'an' depends on the first sound, not the first letter. 'Unique' begins with a consonant 'yoo' sound, so it must be 'a unique excuse', not 'an unique excuse'.

Directions: Each item in this section has a sentence with three parts in square brackets labelled (a), (b) and (c). Read each sentence to determine whether there is an error in any part in square brackets and indicate your response on the answer sheet against the above-mentioned corresponding letter. If there is no error, indicate your response as (d).

[The visiting school children] (a) [went around the lake] (b) [during trip to the famous lake city.] (c) [No error] (d)
c: during trip to the famous lake city.
explanation: 'Trip' is a singular countable noun, so it needs a determiner: 'during a trip' or 'during their trip'. Leaving the article out makes part (c) ungrammatical.

Directions: Each item in this section has a sentence with three parts in square brackets labelled (a), (b) and (c). Read each sentence to determine whether there is an error in any part in square brackets and indicate your response on the answer sheet against the above-mentioned corresponding letter. If there is no error, indicate your response as (d).

[The unfair distribution] (a) [of assets among the family members] (b) [angered the more hardworking members of the family-owned firm.] (c) [No error] (d)
b: of assets among the family members
c: angered the more hardworking members of the family-owned firm.
explanation: The key marks part (c) as wrong. The clearest fault in it is the compound adjective before the noun, which must be hyphenated as 'family-owned firm'. The comparative 'the more hardworking members' is also loosely used, since there is no clear comparison.

Directions: Each item in this section has a sentence with three parts in square brackets labelled (a), (b) and (c). Read each sentence to determine whether there is an error in any part in square brackets and indicate your response on the answer sheet against the above-mentioned corresponding letter. If there is no error, indicate your response as (d).

[Given the nature of the problem] (a) [it was not unnatural for there to be] (b) [bad blood among the two of them.] (c) [No error] (d)
a: Given the nature of the problem
b: it was not unnatural for there to be
c: bad blood among the two of them.
explanation: 'Between' is used for two people or things and 'among' for three or more. Since 'the two of them' refers to exactly two people, it should be 'bad blood between the two of them'.

Directions: Each item in this section has a sentence with three parts in square brackets labelled (a), (b) and (c). [He emphasised the need for] (a) [strict discipline and compliance] (b) [among the newly-appointed staff.] (c) [No error] (d)
explanation: This sentence has no error. 'Emphasised the need for' is the correct idiom, 'strict discipline and compliance' is a correctly paired noun phrase, and 'among the newly-appointed staff' correctly refers to a group of more than two people.

Directions: Each item in this section has a sentence with three parts in square brackets labelled (a), (b) and (c). Read each sentence to determine whether there is an error in any part in square brackets and indicate your response on the answer sheet against the above-mentioned corresponding letter. If there is no error, indicate your response as (d).

[The officer marvelled] (a) [at the low attendance] (b) [remarking on the presence of less than twenty people at work.] (c) [No error] (d)
c: remarking on the presence of less than twenty people at work.
explanation: 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns such as people, and 'less' with uncountable nouns such as water or time. So it should be 'fewer than twenty people'.

Directions: Each item in this section has a sentence with three parts in square brackets labelled (a), (b) and (c). [The entire attention of the visiting] (a) [dignitaries centred around] (b) [the craftwork on display.] (c) [No error] (d)
a: The entire attention of the visiting
explanation: A centre is a single point, so standard usage is 'centred on' (or 'upon'), and 'centred around' is considered illogical. Part (b) is therefore the error.

b: who had trudged for hundreds of kilometres
c: has finally arrived at the destination.
explanation: This sentence has no error. 'A group of…' is a collective subject treated as one unit, so the singular 'has finally arrived' is correct. The past perfect 'had trudged' correctly shows the earlier action.

Directions: Each item in this section has a sentence with three parts in square brackets labelled (a), (b) and (c). a: The tumult among the gathered spectators
c: upon the arrival of their most favourite superstar.
explanation: 'Favourite' already means 'liked most', so it has a superlative sense and cannot take 'most'. It should be 'their favourite superstar'.

a: The listings on the menu that had been proffered by him
c: and discernment with regard to taste and preference.
explanation: This sentence has no error. The plural subject 'listings' agrees with 'were selected', the past perfect 'had been proffered' is used correctly, and 'with regard to' is the correct idiom.

Directions: Each of the following sentences in this section has a blank space with four options. Select whichever preposition or determiner you consider the most appropriate for the blank space and indicate your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Not _____ metal is necessarily solid in its natural state.
explanation: 'Not every' takes a singular countable noun and singular verb ('Not every metal is…'), meaning some metals are not solid, mercury being one. 'Not all' would need the plural 'metals are', and 'not each' or 'not any' are unidiomatic here.

Directions: Each of the following sentences in this section has a blank space with four options. Select whichever preposition or determiner you consider the most appropriate for the blank space and indicate your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

The reminder has gone out on _____ occasions, requiring personnel to complete their personal files.
explanation: 'On several occasions' means more than once, which naturally explains why a reminder had to be sent. 'Further' needs earlier context, 'untold' is an exaggeration, and 'on most occasions' makes no sense for a reminder.

Directions: Each of the following sentences in this section has a blank space with four options. Select whichever preposition or determiner you consider the most appropriate for the blank space and indicate your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

It is important for people to work _____ their co-workers in the office to ensure maximum productivity.
explanation: 'Work with' means to cooperate alongside someone, which suits co-workers aiming for productivity. 'Work for' means to be employed by someone, and 'work over' has a different, negative meaning.

Directions: Each of the following sentences in this section has a blank space with four options. Select whichever preposition or determiner you consider the most appropriate for the blank space and indicate your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

You can choose _____ shirt you like from the collection available in the shop.
explanation: 'Whichever' is used for a choice from a limited, known set, and here the set is the shirts available in the shop. 'Whatever' suggests an open-ended choice, 'whatsoever' is an intensifier, and 'which' alone would need a question structure.

Depending on your preference, you can choose to complete either or _____ courses being offered by the university.
explanation: 'Either or both' is a fixed pairing meaning one of the two or the two together. 'Either' already sets up two options, so only 'both' completes it logically.

Directions: In the following items similar sounding words are given, followed by sentences wherein in each sentence one of these words has been used, and put in square brackets. You are required to identify those sentences in which these words have been used most appropriately and mark your response in the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Dairy, Dreary, Diary
1. She quietly stored all her sacred memories in her private [dairy].
2. The proceedings of the meeting went on and on and were quite [dreary].
3. They always bought their milk products from the local [diary].
In which of the sentences given above has/have the words been used correctly ?
explanation: Only sentence 2 is correct, because 'dreary' means dull and tiresome. Sentences 1 and 3 swap the words: memories go in a 'diary' (a personal record), and milk products come from a 'dairy'.

Directions: In the following items similar sounding words are given, followed by sentences wherein in each sentence one of these words has been used, and put in square brackets. You are required to identify those sentences in which these words have been used most appropriately and mark your response in the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Braid, Beard, Brood
1. The engineers were asked to [braid] the river by converting it into single body with the aid of an artificial dam.
2. Wise men, they say, often sport a [beard].
3. Among certain avian species the males are known to [brood] the eggs laid by females.
In which of the sentences given above has/have the words been used correctly ?
explanation: A 'beard' fits sentence 2, and 'brood' (to sit on eggs to hatch them) is correct in sentence 3, since in some birds the male does this. Sentence 1 is wrong because to 'braid' means to interweave strands, the opposite of merging a river into a single body.

You are required to identify those sentences in which these words have been used most appropriately and mark your response in the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Lesion, Legion, Lesson
1. The scan of the affected area indicated the presence of a life-threatening [lesion].
2. He had a [legion] of followers who hung on to his every word.
3. It is important to [lesson] the burden of others as we venture through life.
In which of the sentences given above has/have the words been used correctly ?
explanation: A 'lesion' is an abnormal area of tissue that a scan can show, and a 'legion' is a vast number, so sentences 1 and 2 are correct. Sentence 3 needs the verb 'lessen' (reduce), not 'lesson'.

Directions: In the following items similar sounding words are given, followed by sentences wherein in each sentence one of these words has been used, and put in square brackets. You are required to identify those sentences in which these words have been used most appropriately and mark your response in the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Depose, Deplore, Deport
1. The director asked the actor to [depose] himself and instead act naturally.
2. The people are enthusiastically declaring that they [deplore] the salutary impact of the decisions taken by the administration.
3. Under extreme circumstances, the government can [deport] someone from a country.
In which of the sentences given above has/have the words been used correctly ?
explanation: Only sentence 3 is correct, because to 'deport' is to expel someone from a country. To 'depose' means to remove from office (the actor should 'compose' himself), and one cannot 'deplore' (strongly condemn) a salutary, beneficial impact with enthusiasm.

You are required to identify those sentences in which these words have been used most appropriately and mark your response in the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Bate, Bait, Bade
1. Those who had gathered for the unveiling were asked to [bate] their curiosity.
2. They set the [bait] to capture the leopard for tagging.
3. He reluctantly [bade] goodbye to his belongings.
In which of the sentences given above has/have the words been used correctly ?
explanation: All three are correct. To 'bate' is to restrain or hold back (as in 'bated breath'), 'bait' is food used to lure an animal, and 'bade' is the past tense of 'bid', as in 'bade goodbye'.

Someone's ears are flapping
a: Someone in a state of intense agitation
b: Someone in a state of heightened excitement
c: Someone desperate to eavesdrop on a conversation
d: Someone embarrassed at being caught in the act of lying
explanation: 'Someone's ears are flapping' describes a person eagerly trying to overhear a conversation that does not concern them. It is about eavesdropping, not agitation or excitement.

Directions: In the following items an idiom or a proverb is given. Select the response that most appropriately describes the meaning of the idiom or proverb and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Twist of the knife
a: Slicing through the difficulties that one faces in life
b: To accept defeat in the face of an enemy
c: The last thrust of a difficult operation
d: To make someone who is already feeling bad, feel worse with one's words or actions
explanation: To 'twist the knife (in the wound)' is to make someone who is already hurt feel worse through further words or actions. It has nothing to do with overcoming difficulties or finishing an operation.

Blow your own trumpet
b: All sound and fury, signifying nothing
c: Excessively boastful of one's own achievements
d: Be scathing in one's criticism of others
explanation: To 'blow your own trumpet' is to boast about your own achievements. It is about self-praise, not loudness or criticising others.

Directions: In the following items an idiom or a proverb is given. Select the response that most appropriately describes the meaning of the idiom or proverb and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Get under someone's skin
a: To fall intensely in love with someone
b: To cause intense liking in someone
d: To annoy or irritate someone intensely
explanation: To 'get under someone's skin' usually means to annoy or irritate them persistently. It does not mean understanding someone completely, and the romantic sense is not the standard meaning tested.

Many hands make light work
a: Many people working together can light a new path
b: Many people helping can help accomplish a task quickly
c: Many people working together can make work non-serious
d: Workers light up the work they undertake
explanation: The proverb means that when many people share a task, it is finished quickly and easily. 'Light' here means 'not heavy', not illumination or lack of seriousness.

Directions: In the following items an idiom or a proverb is given. Select the response that most appropriately describes the meaning of the idiom or proverb and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

A bird in hand is worth two in the bush
a: What's hidden is always a matter of speculation
b: What we have is always more valuable that what we have a chance of getting
c: A gift is always better kept close to oneself
d: What can happen is always better than what has happened
explanation: The proverb advises that something you already have is worth more than a bigger gain you might get but are not sure of. Option (d) reverses this, valuing possibility over what is certain.

Make heavy weather
c: To complain about wet and rainy conditions
d: Unnecessarily create difficulty in dealing with a task
explanation: To 'make heavy weather of' something is to make a task seem harder than it is, or to handle it with needless difficulty. It has nothing to do with actual weather.

Directions: In the following items an idiom or a proverb is given. Select the response that most appropriately describes the meaning of the idiom or proverb and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Sweep under the carpet
c: Keep a problem under wraps in the hope that it will be forgotten
d: Do a quick clean up job
explanation: To 'sweep (something) under the carpet' is to hide a problem or scandal in the hope that it will be forgotten. Option (b) 'hide from general view' leaves out the key idea of avoiding a problem.

Directions: In the following items an idiom or a proverb is given. Select the response that most appropriately describes the meaning of the idiom or proverb and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

A purple patch
b: The final bloom of the season
c: A great run of luck or success or form
d: A bodily discolouration related to heredity
explanation: A 'purple patch' is a period of exceptional success, good luck or good form, as with a batsman scoring heavily in several matches. It has nothing to do with flowers or skin colour.

text:
Directions: In the following items an idiom or a proverb is given. Select the response that most appropriately describes the meaning of the idiom or proverb and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

Put out to pasture
explanation: To 'put out to pasture' means to retire someone or something as no longer useful, as old farm animals were turned out to graze. It does not literally mean feeding someone.

Directions: In the following items a pair of sentences (S1, S2) is given. Select the most appropriate and relevant co-relationship of the second sentence to the first from among the options (a), (b), (c) and (d), and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

S1 : Failure is the stepping stone to success.
S2 : Successive failures are not however successive stepping stones to success.
The second sentence :
a: contradicts the wisdom of the first
b: contrasts the wisdom of the first
c: confirms the wisdom of the first
d: qualifies the wisdom of the first
explanation: S2 accepts S1 but limits its scope: failure can lead to success, yet repeated failures do not keep adding up to it. Narrowing a statement without rejecting it is 'qualifying' it, not contradicting it.

S1 : All human beings are created equal in every respect.
S2 : Some people are more equal than others.
The second sentence :
explanation: S1 says all people are equal in every respect, while S2 says some are more equal than others. S2 directly denies S1, so it contradicts it.

Directions: In the following items a pair of sentences (S1, S2) is given. Select the most appropriate and relevant co-relationship of the second sentence to the first from among the options (a), (b), (c) and (d), and mark your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly.

a: contradicts the assertion made in the first

explanation: S2 states as a general principle what S1 gives as an example: the highest clouds are the most out of reach, and therefore the most fascinating. S2 restates, or reiterates, the same idea.

S1 : A four-stroke engine is more efficient than a two-stroke engine.
S2 : The two-stroke engine has been phased out to protect the environment.
The second sentence :
explanation: Both sentences are about the relative merits of the two engine types. The lower efficiency of the two-stroke engine in S1 links logically to its phasing out in S2, so S2 correlates to S1 without confirming or contradicting it.

S1 : Bottled water is safer than tap water.
S2 : In many countries tap water is fed to babies.
The second sentence :
d: is an extension of the first
explanation: S2 suggests that tap water is safe enough for babies in many countries, which stands in contrast to S1's claim that bottled water is safer. It does not refute S1 outright, so 'contrasts with' is better than 'contradicts'.

d: provides escalatory information to what is contained in the first
explanation: S2 adds a related fact on the same theme (a state bird alongside the national bird) without disputing S1. It simply provides additional information.

S1 : Field games are generally more popular than individual sports.
S2 : Across the world tennis is more popular than hockey.
The second sentence :
